Mercedes-Benz's New Electric Two-Seater Chassis Mule Sure Looks Weird, Is the SLC Coming Back?
14 photos
Photo: Baldauf
Could Mercedes be working on an electric roadster here, probably an electric take on the SLC as an alternative to the Porsche 718 Boxster in full-electric specification? We don't know for certain, but from the looks of it, a two-seater chassis test mule with a rear-mounted electric drive unit suggests exactly that.
There is no bodywork to speak of, no doors, and no windshield either. Barely anything resembles a cabin at this point, and the amount of plywood used to make this mule happen beggars belief. Built around a black-painted frame, the vehicle also shows exposed suspension componentry and a rear-mounted battery.
Said high-voltage pack is relatively small and is located right behind the rear motor. It literally hangs out beyond the rear axle, which is the kind of location that made me remember the Ford Pinto scandal from the 1970s. The TL;DR version is a fuel tank design flaw that made the American subcompact prone to catching fire in rear-end collisions.
The battery's location is all the more weird once you remember that Porsche went in a completely different direction with the zero-emission 718 range . Instead of packaging the high-voltage pack underfloor, as you'd expect from a conventional electric vehicle, the E-Core layout mounts the battery behind the rear seats, mimicking a mid-engine configuration.
Stacking it vertically behind the rear seats definitely helps with weight distribution, but this layout also enables a low seating position and reproduces the polar moment of inertia of a mid-engine sports car. Porsche's battery uses three modules stacked across two vertical levels, and curiously enough, it rocks prismatic cells instead of cylindrical cells.
Photo: Baldauf Accommodating two people, the Mercedes test mule is pictured with a laptop in the passenger's lap. Definitely a work in progress, the open-top mule features pretty substantial rear control arms and unusually high front suspension mounts. We can further see how the steering column sits unusually far back, indicating a very long hood for whatever production model may transpire from this fellow.
All of these elements, combined with the relatively short wheelbase, made us wonder if an electric SL or SLC is under development. The SLC route seems the most plausible, and there is some historical context to back the roadster hunch up.
Back in 2021, then development chief Markus Schaefer confirmed that AMG was considering an electric ragtop . Schaefer stepped down as CTO last year, leaving the company in December 2025. While Schaefer acknowledged that the business case was difficult to make due to declining demand for such vehicles, he nevertheless considered the open-top electric AMG an appealing proposition.
The automaker's electric vehicle strategy has shifted dramatically since 2021, with Mercedes favoring combustion and hybrid alternatives alongside electric models nowadays. Mercedes hasn't confirmed the existence of this odd platform or named a future application for it, making the e-roadster mule all the more mysterious.
